facts.text: Speed describes how fast something moves, acceleration describes how quickly its speed increases, and deceleration describes how quickly its speed decreases.
facts.quote: Speed is how fast something moves, acceleration is how quickly its speed increases, and deceleration is how quickly its speed decreases.

facts.text: To convert speed from km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6: 15 km/h is about 4.2 m/s, 30 km/h about 8.3 m/s, and 50 km/h about 13.9 m/s.
facts.quote: To convert, divide km/h by 3.6: 15 km/h is about 4.2 m/s, 30 km/h about 8.3 m/s, 50 km/h about 13.9 m/s.

facts.text: The machines covered by the booklet mostly operate between 3 and 15 km/h; haul trucks reach 30 to 50 km/h on haul roads.
facts.quote: The machines in the booklet mostly work between 3 and 15 km/h, and haul trucks reach 30 to 50 km/h on haul roads.

facts.text: A machine decelerating at 2 m/s² loses 2 m/s of speed each second and would stop from 4.2 m/s after about 2.1 seconds.
facts.quote: A deceleration of 2 m/s² means the machine loses 2 m/s of speed every second: from 4.2 m/s it would stand still after about 2.1 seconds.

facts.text: The acceleration unit g is about 9.81 m/s².
facts.quote: g, the acceleration of a freely falling object, about 9.81 m/s².

facts.text: The road-car automatic braking regulation UN R152 demands at least 5.0 m/s² deceleration, about 0.5 g.
facts.quote: The road-car automatic braking regulation UN Regulation No. 152 demands at least 5.0 m/s², about 0.5 g [Chapter 8].

facts.text: New South Wales guidance proposes a minimum in-service deceleration of 0.60 m/s², about 0.06 g, for heavy off-road machines.
facts.quote: New South Wales guidance proposes a minimum in-service deceleration of 0.60 m/s² (about 0.06 g)

facts.text: The US mining rule in MSHA Table M-1 assumes constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s², about 2.94 m/s² or 0.3 g; MSHA is the US Mine Safety and Health Administration.
facts.quote: the US mining rule in MSHA Table M-1 (MSHA is the US Mine Safety and Health Administration) assumes a constant 9.66 ft/s², about 2.94 m/s² or 0.3 g

entities.name: US Mine Safety and Health Administration

facts.text: A South African industry specification sets emergency-stop deceleration at 1.9 m/s² for machines faster than 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for slower machines.
facts.quote: a South African industry specification sets an emergency-stop deceleration of 1.9 m/s² for machines faster than 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for slower ones [Chapters 7, 8].

facts.text: A loaded haul truck may decelerate at less than one-third of a car's deceleration rate.
facts.quote: A loaded haul truck may decelerate at less than a third of the rate of a car.

facts.text: Decelerating a 40 t machine at 3 m/s² requires brake force of 120,000 N, or 120 kN; brake torque and brake heat limit heavy machines.
facts.quote: To decelerate a 40 t machine at 3 m/s² the brakes must supply 40,000 x 3 = 120,000 N, or 120 kN, roughly the weight of a 12 t object; that is why brake torque and brake heat limit heavy machines.

facts.text: The booklet recommends gradually ramping up deceleration with a jerk limit because sudden stops jolt operators and shift loads; jerk is the rate of change of acceleration.
facts.quote: And jerk is the rate of change of acceleration: how suddenly the braking comes on. The booklet recommends ramping deceleration up gradually, with a jerk limit, because sudden stops jolt operators and shift loads [Chapters 4, 8].

facts.text: Every stopping-distance calculation in the booklet uses speed, deceleration and time; confusing km/h with m/s or g with m/s² produces errors of a factor of three or ten.
facts.quote: Every stopping-distance calculation in the booklet is built from speed, deceleration and time, so misreading a unit (km/h for m/s, or g for m/s²) produces errors of a factor of three or ten.

facts.text: Regulatory sources use different deceleration definitions: UN R152 uses commanded braking demand, ISO 3450 uses mean deceleration computed from stopping distance, MSHA uses constant deceleration with separate response times, and New South Wales uses net deceleration on grade.
facts.quote: a commanded braking demand (UN R152), a mean deceleration computed from stopping distance (ISO 3450), a constant deceleration with separate response times (MSHA) and a net deceleration on grade (New South Wales).

entities.name: US Mine Safety and Health Administration

facts.text: A program pooling deceleration values from regulatory sources must first convert those values to one deceleration definition.
facts.quote: A program that pools them must first convert them to one definition [Chapter 8].
